text: NemoFleet. How a robot fleet can teach itself in passing, using two ideas from nature: duck feet and ant trails.
Today, when a robot is unsure, it asks the big model in the cloud. Every robot, every time, even when another robot solved the same problem a minute ago. That is slow, and it burns GPU.

A duck standing on ice has a similar problem with heat. Its trick is countercurrent exchange. Warm blood flowing down to the foot runs right beside cold blood flowing back up. At every point the warm side is a little warmer, so heat keeps crossing over the whole way. The foot stays cold, the body stays warm, and very little heat is wasted.

If the two flows ran in the same direction, they would simply meet in the middle. Running them in opposite directions keeps a small gap everywhere, so the cold side ends up nearly as warm as the hot side.
Now swap heat for knowledge. Trained robots are hot. New robots are cold. And the energy we want to save is cloud compute, spent re-solving problems the fleet has already solved.

Option A is the countercurrent curriculum. A scheduler routes trained robots out toward the edge, and new robots in toward the core. Each new robot first passes peers only slightly ahead of it, then progressively more expert ones. Every pass carries a small difference that is easy to absorb. New robots warm up quickly, and only what no peer can answer goes to Ultra.
Ants solve a different part of the problem. Every time two ants pass on a trail, they touch antennae and swap news. Outbound ants learn what is ahead. Returning ants carry status home.

Option B is ant-trail antennation. Robots do a quick handshake whenever they pass. Here, a spill appears near the frontier. Only the first robot to see it calls Cosmos to understand it. After that, the news travels robot to robot. Hazard tags on the map fade over time, and the depot sends Ultra a short digest instead of a raw stream.
Together, A decides who passes whom, and B decides what they say. One rule never bends. If a person is in the lane, the robot always escalates to Ultra, whatever its peers say.

We will test this on Nebius Serverless Jobs, comparing countercurrent pairing with random pairing and with no peers at all. We will count Ultra calls per new problem, and how fast a hazard reaches the whole fleet. Cold feet, warm core. That is NemoFleet.
